    ffHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    ffHelpS1P1: 'Free fall is the motion of a body under the influence of Earth\'s gravity alone, neglecting air resistance. In this case, all bodies (regardless of mass) acquire the same constant acceleration, called gravitational acceleration, denoted by g.',
    ffHelpS1P2: 'This motion follows the equations of linear motion with constant acceleration. If the body starts from rest (initial velocity v₀ = 0) and falls a vertical distance y in time t, the equation relating distance to time is:',
    ffHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    ffHelpS2M1: 'Distance-time equation: y = ½ · g · t²',
    ffHelpS2M2: 'Final velocity-time equation: v = g · t',
    ffHelpS2M3: 'Velocity-distance equation: v² = 2 · g · y',
    ffHelpS2M4: 'Extracting g from one measurement: g = 2y / t²',
    ffHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual or Real)',
    ffHelpS3L1: 'Equipment setup: Mount the graduated ruler vertically, place the ball (or falling object) at the starting point (zero height), and prepare the electronic timer (or photogates for precise time measurement).',

    ffHelpS3L3: 'Release & measure: Let the object fall freely (from rest), and record the time (t) taken to reach the ground or photogate.',
    ffHelpS3L4: 'Repetition: Repeat the step for each height 3 times and calculate the average time to reduce experimental error.',
    ffHelpS3L5: 'Square the time: Calculate the square of the average time (t²) for each height.',
    ffHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    ffHelpS4P1: 'To find the value of gravitational acceleration (g) scientifically from the graph:',
    ffHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot distance (y) on the Y-axis. Plot time squared (t²) on the X-axis.',
    ffHelpS4L2: 'Slope: When plotting the relationship, you get a straight line through the origin. Calculate its slope: Slope = Δy / Δt²',
    ffHelpS4L3: 'Calculating g: Comparing with the theoretical equation (y = ½gt²), the slope equals half the gravitational acceleration: Slope = ½ · g → g = 2 × Slope',

    coHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',

    coHelpS1P3: 'Collision in this experiment is divided into two main types:',
    coHelpS1L1: 'Elastic Collision: Both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved (bodies bounce off each other).',
    coHelpS1L2: 'Perfectly Inelastic Collision: Momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy is lost (bodies stick together and move as one mass after collision).',
    coHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    coHelpS2P1: 'General momentum conservation law:',
    coHelpS2P2: '(where i means before collision, and f means after collision).',
    coHelpS2P3: 'For perfectly inelastic collision (masses stick together):',
    coHelpS2P4: 'The shared velocity after collision (v_f):',
    coHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    coHelpS3P1: 'We apply the perfectly inelastic collision where the second cart is initially at rest to simplify calculations:',
    coHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Choose two carts, first with mass (m₁) and second with mass (m₂). Keep the second cart completely stationary (v₂ᵢ = 0).',
    coHelpS3L2: 'Set initial velocity: Push the first cart with a known initial velocity (v₁ᵢ) toward the second cart.',
    coHelpS3L3: 'Collision & sticking: The first cart collides with the second and they stick together using tape or magnets, moving as one body.',
    coHelpS3L4: 'Measure final velocity: Measure the shared velocity of both carts after collision (v_f) using photogates or motion sensors.',
    coHelpS3L5: 'Repeat: Change the first mass (m₁) several times while keeping the second cart mass (m₂) and initial velocity (v₁ᵢ) constant, and record the final velocity (v_f) each time.',
    coHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    coHelpS4P1: 'To prove the momentum conservation law graphically and find the fixed mass (m₂) as unknown:',
    coHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot total initial momentum (pᵢ = m₁ · v₁ᵢ) on the Y-axis. Plot shared final velocity (v_f) on the X-axis.',

    coHelpS4L3: 'Calculating the unknown: Since pᵢ = p_f = (m₁ + m₂) · v_f, the slope represents the sum of masses: Slope = m₁ + m₂. If the second cart mass (m₂) is unknown, it can be calculated: m₂ = Slope - m₁',

    coHelpS6L2: 'Understanding how kinetic energy dissipates and transforms into other forms (heat, structural deformation, sound) in inelastic collisions.',

    // ── Lever Help Modal ──
    lvHelpTitle: '⚖️ Force Equilibrium Resultant Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    lvHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    lvHelpS1P1: 'Force is a vector quantity with magnitude and direction. When multiple forces act on a body simultaneously, the overall effect is called the Resultant Force.',
    lvHelpS1P2: 'For a body to be in Static Equilibrium, the first equilibrium condition must be satisfied: the vector sum of all forces acting on the body must equal zero:',
    lvHelpS1P3: 'In this experiment, if two forces (F⃗₁ and F⃗₂) act on a central ring, their resultant (F_R) requires a third force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction called the Equilibrant Force (F⃗_E):',
    lvHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used (Component Analysis)',
    lvHelpS2P1: 'To find the resultant analytically, we resolve each force into two components (horizontal and vertical):',
    lvHelpS2M1: 'Horizontal components (X): ΣFₓ = F₁·cos(θ₁) + F₂·cos(θ₂)',
    lvHelpS2M2: 'Vertical components (Y): ΣFᵧ = F₁·sin(θ₁) + F₂·sin(θ₂)',
    lvHelpS2M3: 'Resultant magnitude (F_R): F_R = √(ΣFₓ² + ΣFᵧ²)',
    lvHelpS2M4: 'Resultant direction (φ): φ = tan⁻¹(ΣFᵧ / ΣFₓ)',
    lvHelpS2M5: 'Equilibrant angle: θ_E = φ + 180°',
    lvHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    lvHelpS3L1: 'Define two forces: Choose two force values (via known masses, where F = m·g) and two different angles (e.g., F₁ = 2 N at 0°, F₂ = 3 N at 120°).',
    lvHelpS3L2: 'Observe imbalance: The central ring moves away from center due to the resultant force.',
    lvHelpS3L3: 'Experimental balancing: Add masses (third force F_E) and gradually change its angle until the central ring returns to center, free and not touching the central axis.',
    lvHelpS3L4: 'Record results: Record the magnitude of the third force and the angle that achieved complete equilibrium.',
    lvHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis & Calculating the Unknown',
    lvHelpS4P1: 'In this experiment, we use the Vector Polygon / Parallelogram Method to verify the unknown:',
    lvHelpS4L1: 'Parallelogram method: Choose a suitable scale (e.g., 1 N = 2 cm). Draw vector F⃗₁ at its angle, and from the same origin draw F⃗₂ at its angle. Complete the parallelogram. The diagonal from the origin represents the resultant graphically (F⃗_R).',
    lvHelpS4L2: 'Calculating the unknown: Measure the diagonal length with a ruler and convert to Newtons, measure its angle with a protractor. Compare graphical and theoretical values with the equilibrant force (F_E) found experimentally to verify: F_E = F_R and θ_E = φ ± 180°',
    lvHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    lvHelpS5E1: 'Independent variables: Magnitudes and angles of the first and second forces (F₁, θ₁, F₂, θ₂)',
    lvHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variables: Equilibrant force and its angle (F_E, θ_E) needed to achieve equilibrium',
    lvHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Gravitational acceleration (g) and the central equilibrium point',
    lvHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    lvHelpS6L1: 'Applied understanding of vector addition geometrically and analytically rather than simple algebraic addition.',
    lvHelpS6L2: 'Understanding principles of statics and equilibrium, the fundamental principle in civil and architectural engineering for designing bridges and buildings to prevent collapse under forces.',

    miHelpTitle: '🪞 Spherical Mirrors Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    miHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    miHelpS1P1: 'Spherical mirrors are divided into two types based on the reflecting surface:',
    miHelpS1L1: 'Concave (Converging) Mirror: The reflecting surface is curved inward. It converges parallel rays to a point called the real focal point (F). Image characteristics change (real inverted, or virtual magnified) depending on object position relative to the focal point.',
    miHelpS1L2: 'Convex (Diverging) Mirror: The reflecting surface is curved outward. It diverges incident rays, forming a virtual focal point (F) behind the mirror. Image characteristics are always the same (virtual, upright, diminished) regardless of object position.',
    miHelpS1P2: 'The fundamental principle is based on the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applied to a curved surface, where object distance (u) and image distance (v) are related to the mirror focal length (f).',
    miHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    miHelpS2P1: 'Mirror Equation:',
    miHelpS2P2: '(where u is the object distance from the mirror pole, v is the image distance, and f is the focal length).',
    miHelpS2P3: 'Sign Convention:',
    miHelpS2L1: 'u is always positive for real objects.',
    miHelpS2L2: 'f is positive for concave mirrors, negative for convex mirrors.',
    miHelpS2L3: 'v is positive if the image is real (in front of mirror), negative if virtual (behind mirror).',
    miHelpS2P4: 'Magnification (M):',
    miHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    miHelpS3P1: 'We focus on the concave mirror because it allows obtaining real images that can be received on a screen:',
    miHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Place a light source (arrow-shaped object or candle) in front of a concave mirror with unknown focal length.',
    miHelpS3L2: 'Set object distance (u): Place the object at a known first distance (e.g., u = 30 cm) such that the distance is greater than the expected focal length.',
    miHelpS3L3: 'Determine image distance (v): Move the screen in front of the mirror back and forth until the sharpest inverted image forms on it, then measure the distance from mirror to screen accurately and record it as (v).',
    miHelpS3L4: 'Repeat: Change the object distance (u) to several different values (35 cm, 40 cm, 45 cm, 50 cm), and each time find the corresponding image distance (v) and record data in a table.',
    miHelpS3L5: 'Reciprocals: Calculate the reciprocal of object distance (1/u) and image distance (1/v) for each reading.',
    miHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    miHelpS4P1: 'The goal of the graphical analysis is to find the unknown focal length of the mirror (f).',
    miHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot reciprocal of image distance (1/v) on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of object distance (1/u) on the X-axis.',
    miHelpS4L2: 'Graph nature & slope: You get a straight line sloping downward (inverse relationship between reciprocals), with slope equal to −1: Slope = −1',
    miHelpS4L3: 'Calculating f: From the mirror equation: 1/v = −1/u + 1/f. The Y-intercept and X-intercept both represent 1/f. Read the Y-intercept (let its value be C). Calculate the unknown focal length: f = 1/C',
    miHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    miHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable: Object distance from mirror (u)',
    miHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable: Formed image distance (v)',
    miHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Mirror focal length (f), radius of curvature (R = 2f), and original object height (hₒ)',
    miHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    miHelpS6L1: 'Determining the focal length and radius of curvature of spherical mirrors practically.',
    miHelpS6L2: 'Understanding different image formation cases based on object position relative to center of curvature (C) and focal point (F).',
    miHelpS6L3: 'Practical applications include using concave mirrors in car headlights and telescopes to collect light, and using convex mirrors on car sides and road corners to provide a wide field of view.',

    // ── Prism Help Modal ──
    prHelpTitle: '🌈 Prism Dispersion Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    prHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    prHelpS1P1: 'This experiment relies on the phenomenon of Dispersion. When white light (like sunlight) passes from a medium with a small refractive index (air) to a medium with a larger refractive index (glass or acrylic prism), it undergoes Refraction.',
    prHelpS1P2: 'White light is not a single color, but a mixture of the seven visible spectrum colors. The fundamental physical principle here is that the refractive index of glass (n) depends on the wavelength (λ) of light passing through it, known as Cauchy\'s Equation:',
    prHelpS1P3: 'Since different colors have different wavelengths:',
    prHelpS1L1: 'Red light: Has the largest wavelength (λ), thus encounters the lowest refractive index, making it the least deviated color.',
    prHelpS1L2: 'Violet light: Has the shortest wavelength (λ), thus encounters the highest refractive index, making it the most deviated color.',
    prHelpS1P4: 'Due to this difference in refraction angles, white light exits the prism dispersed into the seven spectrum colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).',
    prHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    prHelpS2P1: 'Snell\'s Law:',
    prHelpS2P2: 'Angle of Deviation (δ): The angle between the incident ray extension and the emerging ray from the prism, calculated at minimum deviation position:',
    prHelpS2P3: '(where A is the prism apex angle, and δₘ is the minimum angle of deviation).',
    prHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    prHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Place the glass prism in the light path, and have the light source emit a narrow beam of white light.',
    prHelpS3L2: 'Observe dispersion: Adjust the incidence angle until the light beam exits the other end of the prism clearly dispersed into rainbow colors on the dark screen.',
    prHelpS3L3: 'Change light type (for calculations): For precise data, switch the light source to monochromatic light, starting with a specific color (e.g., red, where wavelength is precisely known λ ≈ 650 nm).',
    prHelpS3L4: 'Measure deviation angle: Gradually change the incidence angle until reaching the minimum possible deviation angle for the emerging ray, and record the minimum deviation angle (δₘ).',
    prHelpS3L5: 'Repeat for other colors: Repeat with different colors (yellow, green, blue, violet) and record δₘ for each, then use the prism equation to calculate the refractive index (n) for each color (wavelength).',
    prHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    prHelpS4P1: 'The goal is to find the relationship between refractive index and wavelength to verify the prism material constants (Cauchy constants A and B).',
    prHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Calculate the reciprocal of squared wavelength (1/λ²) for each color. Plot refractive index (n) on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of squared wavelength (1/λ²) on the X-axis.',
    prHelpS4L2: 'Slope: You get a straight line rising upward, its slope represents constant B in Cauchy\'s equation: Slope = Δn / Δ(1/λ²) = B',
    prHelpS4L3: 'Calculating the unknown: Constant B = slope value directly. Constant A (refractive index at infinite wavelength) = Y-intercept',
    prHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    prHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable: Wavelength of the used beam (λ)',
    prHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable: Minimum deviation angle (δₘ) and thus refractive index (n)',
    prHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Prism apex angle (A), and glass material',
    prHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    prHelpS6L1: 'Understanding the nature of white light and proving it consists of multiple spectral components.',
    prHelpS6L2: 'Calculating material refractive indices precisely based on colors.',
    prHelpS6L3: 'Practical applications include manufacturing spectrometers used for material analysis, and determining chemical composition of distant stars by analyzing their received light.',
    // ── Diffraction Help Modal ──
    dfHelpTitle: '🔮 Light Diffraction Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    dfHelpS1Title: '🔧 1. Detailed Apparatus Description',
    dfHelpS1L1: 'Optical Bench: A long graduated metal rail on which all components are mounted to ensure perfect alignment on a single optical axis and prevent any lateral ray deviation.',
    dfHelpS1L2: 'Monochromatic Laser Source: Preferably a red laser (known wavelength, e.g., λ = 632.8 nm) or green laser. Its advantage is producing a coherent beam with constant phase and wavelength, essential for clear diffraction patterns.',
    dfHelpS1L3: 'Diffraction Slit Disk/Plate: A glass or metal slide containing precise micrometer-sized openings. In this experiment we use a Single Slit with known width denoted (a) measured in micrometers (μm).',
    dfHelpS1L4: 'Observation Screen: A flat white screen placed at a relatively large distance from the slit, where diffraction fringes (bright and dark regions) appear clearly.',
    dfHelpS1L5: 'Digital Caliper / Micrometer: A very precise measuring tool used to measure distances between dark fringes on the screen with high accuracy in millimeters.',
    dfHelpS2Title: '🔬 2. Detailed Scientific Theory',
    dfHelpS2P1: 'According to traditional geometric optics, light travels in straight lines, so if it passes through a small slit it should appear on the screen as a bright rectangle with the same dimensions as the slit. But in reality, when the slit width (a) is very small and close to the light wavelength (λ), light bends and spreads at the slit edges in different directions; this phenomenon is called Diffraction.',
    dfHelpS2P2: 'The secondary waves resulting from light bending (based on Huygens\' principle) interfere to form a distinctive pattern on the screen called a Diffraction Pattern, consisting of:',
    dfHelpS2L1: 'Central Maximum: A very wide bright fringe at the exact center with the highest intensity.',
    dfHelpS2L2: 'Secondary dark and bright fringes: Distributed on both sides of the central maximum, with intensity and fringe width decreasing away from center.',
    dfHelpS2P3: 'The first dark fringe occurs at a vertical distance (y) from center when destructive interference condition is met, meaning path difference equals one full wavelength.',
    dfHelpS3Title: '📐 3. Mathematical Equations Used',
    dfHelpS3P1: 'Condition for dark fringes in diffraction:',
    dfHelpS3P2: '(where a is slit width, θ is diffraction angle, m is dark fringe order m = ±1, ±2, …, and λ is wavelength).',
    dfHelpS3P3: 'Small angle approximation:',
    dfHelpS3P4: 'Linear equation used in the experiment (for first order m=1):',
    dfHelpS4Title: '⚗️ 4. Detailed Laboratory Procedure',
    dfHelpS4L1: 'Setup and calibration: Mount the laser at the start of the optical bench, followed by the slit holder, then place the white screen at the end at a large known distance (measure distance D between slit and screen with a ruler and keep it constant, e.g., D = 1.5 meter).',
    dfHelpS4L2: 'System operation: Turn on the laser beam and aim it precisely through the first single slit with known width (start with the narrowest slit, e.g., a = 0.04 mm).',
    dfHelpS4L3: 'Observe and read pattern: You will notice a horizontal line of bright and dark fringes on the screen. Identify the center of the central bright maximum, then use the digital caliper to measure the distance from center to the first dark fringe (m=1) on the right side, and record this distance as (y). (For better precision, measure the distance between the first dark fringes on both sides and divide by 2).',
    dfHelpS4L4: 'Change slit width: Rotate the slit disk to switch to another single slit with a different larger width (0.08 mm, 0.12 mm, 0.16 mm), and each time measure the corresponding first dark fringe distance (y). You will notice experimentally that as the slit widens, the diffraction pattern narrows and fringes move closer to center.',
    dfHelpS4L5: 'Calculations: Arrange slit width values (a) in a table, then calculate the reciprocal of slit width (1/a) for all readings to prepare for linear plotting.',
    dfHelpS5Title: '📊 5. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    dfHelpS5P1: 'The goal of the graph is to verify the wave nature and extract the laser wavelength (λ) as an experimental unknown.',
    dfHelpS5L1: 'Axes: Plot first dark fringe distance (y) in millimeters on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of slit width (1/a) in inverse millimeters on the X-axis.',
    dfHelpS5L2: 'Slope: You get a straight line passing through the origin showing direct proportionality between y and (1/a), calculate its slope: Slope = Δy / Δ(1/a)',
    dfHelpS5L3: 'Calculating λ: By comparison with the theoretical equation (y = λD · 1/a), we find the slope equals: Slope = λ · D. Since the screen distance (D) is known and constant, extract the unknown wavelength: λ = Slope / D',
    dfHelpS6Title: '⚙️ 6. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    dfHelpS6E1: 'Independent variable: Single slit width (a) and thus its reciprocal (1/a)',
    dfHelpS6E2: 'Dependent variable: Position or distance of first dark fringe from center (y)',
    dfHelpS6E3: 'Constants: Distance between slit and screen (D), and laser wavelength (λ)',
    dfHelpS7Title: '🎯 7. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    dfHelpS7L1: 'Definitively proving the wave behavior of light and refuting the idea that light travels in absolutely straight lines at microscopic edges.',
    dfHelpS7L2: 'The ability to measure very small dimensions (such as light wavelengths or thin wire and hair diameters) with micrometer precision by observing their diffraction patterns.',
    dfHelpS7L3: 'Enormous technological applications; setting fundamental limits for microscope resolution, controlling electronic chip and processor design (Photolithography), and used in studying crystalline structure of materials via X-ray diffraction.',

    spHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    spHelpS1P1: 'When a mass (m) is hung on a vertically suspended spring, the mass pulls the spring downward with its weight, while an opposing elastic force is generated in the spring trying to restore it to its original position, called the Restoring Force.',
    spHelpS1P2: 'This force follows Hooke\'s Law, which states that the restoring force is directly proportional to the extension (x) in the spring:',
    spHelpS1P3: 'Where (k) is the Spring Constant measured in (N/m). When the mass is displaced from its equilibrium and released, it moves in simple harmonic motion (SHM) up and down with a constant period that depends on the mass and spring stiffness.',
    spHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    spHelpS2M1: 'Hooke\'s Law (static case): m · g = k · x',
    spHelpS2M2: 'Period of spring oscillation (T): T = 2π √(m / k)',
    spHelpS2M3: 'Squaring both sides for a linear relation: T² = (4π² / k) · m',
    spHelpS2M4: 'Angular frequency (ω₀): ω₀ = √(k / m)',
    spHelpS2M5: 'Total energy of the system: E = ½ · k · A²',

    spHelpS3L1: 'Fix the spring: Choose a spring with a specified stiffness constant (k) in the system.',

    spHelpS3L3: 'Start oscillation & measure: Pull the mass down slightly and release. Measure the time of 10 complete oscillations with the digital timer, then divide by 10 to get the period (T) for one mass.',
    spHelpS3L4: 'Repetition: Repeat the steps using different increasing masses (0.2 kg, 0.3 kg, 0.4 kg, 0.5 kg).',

    // ── Projectile Help Modal ──
    pjHelpTitle: '🚀 Projectile Motion Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    pjHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    pjHelpS1P1: 'Projectile motion is the motion of a body launched into the air at an angle under the influence of gravity alone (neglecting air resistance). The fundamental principle here is motion independence, where projectile motion is split into two dimensions (2D):',
    pjHelpS1L1: 'Horizontal motion (X-axis): at constant velocity (vₓ) since no force acts (horizontal acceleration aₓ = 0).',
    pjHelpS1L2: 'Vertical motion (Y-axis): with constant acceleration due to gravity (aᵧ = -g), where velocity decreases during ascent and increases during descent.',
    pjHelpS1P2: 'If the projectile is launched with initial velocity v₀ at angle θ to the horizontal, the velocity components are:',
    pjHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    pjHelpS2M1: 'Horizontal Range (R): R = v₀² · sin(2θ) / g',
    pjHelpS2M2: 'Maximum Height (H): H = v₀² · sin²(θ) / (2g)',
    pjHelpS2M3: 'Total Time of Flight (T): T = 2 · v₀ · sin(θ) / g',
    pjHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    pjHelpS3L1: 'Fix initial velocity: Choose a constant initial velocity (e.g., v₀ = 10 m/s).',
    pjHelpS3L2: 'Change launch angle (θ): Start at 15° then gradually increase (30°, 45°, 60°, 75°).',
    pjHelpS3L3: 'Launch & observe range: Each time, launch the projectile and measure the horizontal range (R) using the lab measurement tool.',
    pjHelpS3L4: 'Record data: Arrange angles and corresponding ranges in a table, then calculate sin(2θ) for each angle.',
    pjHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    pjHelpS4P1: 'To find the initial velocity (v₀) or verify gravitational acceleration (g) graphically:',
    pjHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot horizontal range (R) on the Y-axis. Plot sin(2θ) on the X-axis.',
    pjHelpS4L2: 'Slope: The graph gives a straight line through the origin, its slope is: Slope = ΔR / Δsin(2θ)',
    pjHelpS4L3: 'Calculating the unknown: Comparing with the equation (R = v₀²/g · sin(2θ)), we find: Slope = v₀² / g. If g is known (9.8 m/s²), you can calculate the unknown initial velocity: v₀ = √(Slope × g)',
    pjHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    pjHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable (controlled): Launch angle (θ)',
    pjHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable (changes with angle): Horizontal range (R), and maximum height (H)',

    pjHelpS6L1: 'Proving that maximum horizontal range is always achieved at a launch angle of 45°.',

    inHelpTitle: '📐 Inclined Plane Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    inHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    inHelpS1P1: 'When a body of mass (m) is placed on a surface inclined at angle (θ) to the horizontal, gravity (weight W = m·g) acts vertically downward. To study the motion, we resolve the weight into two perpendicular components relative to the incline surface:',
    inHelpS1L1: 'Component perpendicular to surface (m·g·cosθ): balanced by the normal force (N) exerted by the surface on the body (N = m·g·cosθ).',
    inHelpS1L2: 'Component parallel to surface (m·g·sinθ): the force responsible for pulling the body and making it slide down.',
    inHelpS1P2: 'If the surface is rough, a kinetic friction force (f_k) arises opposing the motion, directed upward parallel to the surface:',
    inHelpS1P3: 'Where (μ_k) is the Coefficient of Kinetic Friction.',
    inHelpS1P4: 'Applying Newton\'s Second Law along the incline (ΣF = m·a):',
    inHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    inHelpS2M1: 'Smooth surface case (μ_k = 0): a = g·sin(θ)',
    inHelpS2M2: 'Rough surface case: a = g·sin(θ) − μ_k·g·cos(θ)',
    inHelpS2M3: 'Motion equation to calculate acceleration practically (from rest): x = ½ · a · t² → a = 2x / t²',
    inHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    inHelpS3P1: 'We focus on the smooth surface to simplify graphical calculations and find gravitational acceleration:',

    inHelpS3L2: 'Change angle (θ): Start with a small angle (e.g., 10°) then gradually increase (20°, 30°, 40°, 50°).',
    inHelpS3L3: 'Measure: Let the body slide from rest from the top of the set distance and record the arrival time (t) with the timer.',

    inHelpS3L5: 'Calculate sine: Calculate sin(θ) for each angle used.',

    inHelpS4P1: 'The goal here is to calculate gravitational acceleration (g) from inclined plane motion.',

    coHelpTitle: '💥 Linear Collision Experiment Guide (1D Collision) — Complete Guide',
    coHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    coHelpS1P1: 'When two bodies collide in an isolated system (no external forces like friction), the Law of Conservation of Momentum states that the total momentum before collision equals the total momentum immediately after collision.',
    coHelpS1P2: 'Momentum (p) is defined as the product of mass and velocity (p = m · v).',
    coHelpS1P3: 'Collision in this experiment is divided into two main types:',
    coHelpS1L1: 'Elastic Collision: Both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved (bodies bounce off each other).',
    coHelpS1L2: 'Perfectly Inelastic Collision: Momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy is lost (bodies stick together and move as one mass after collision).',
    coHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    coHelpS2P1: 'General momentum conservation law:',
    coHelpS2P2: '(where i means before collision, and f means after collision).',

    coHelpS2P4: 'The shared velocity after collision (v_f):',
    coHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    coHelpS3P1: 'We apply the perfectly inelastic collision where the second cart is initially at rest to simplify calculations:',
    coHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Choose two carts, first with mass (m₁) and second with mass (m₂). Keep the second cart completely stationary (v₂ᵢ = 0).',
    coHelpS3L2: 'Set initial velocity: Push the first cart with a known initial velocity (v₁ᵢ) toward the second cart.',
    coHelpS3L3: 'Collision & sticking: The first cart collides with the second and they stick together using tape or magnets, moving as one body.',
    coHelpS3L4: 'Measure final velocity: Measure the shared velocity of both carts after collision (v_f) using photogates or motion sensors.',
    coHelpS3L5: 'Repeat: Change the first mass (m₁) several times while keeping the second cart mass (m₂) and initial velocity (v₁ᵢ) constant, and record the final velocity (v_f) each time.',
    coHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    coHelpS4P1: 'To prove the momentum conservation law graphically and find the fixed mass (m₂) as unknown:',
    coHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot total initial momentum (pᵢ = m₁ · v₁ᵢ) on the Y-axis. Plot shared final velocity (v_f) on the X-axis.',
    coHelpS4L2: 'Slope: You get a straight line through the origin, its slope is: Slope = Δpᵢ / Δv_f',
    coHelpS4L3: 'Calculating the unknown: Since pᵢ = p_f = (m₁ + m₂) · v_f, the slope represents the sum of masses: Slope = m₁ + m₂. If the second cart mass (m₂) is unknown, it can be calculated: m₂ = Slope - m₁',

    // ── Lever Help Modal ──
    lvHelpTitle: '⚖️ Force Equilibrium Resultant Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    lvHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    lvHelpS1P1: 'Force is a vector quantity with magnitude and direction. When multiple forces act on a body simultaneously, the overall effect is called the Resultant Force.',
    lvHelpS1P2: 'For a body to be in Static Equilibrium, the first equilibrium condition must be satisfied: the vector sum of all forces acting on the body must equal zero:',
    lvHelpS1P3: 'In this experiment, if two forces (F⃗₁ and F⃗₂) act on a central ring, their resultant (F_R) requires a third force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction called the Equilibrant Force (F⃗_E):',
    lvHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used (Component Analysis)',
    lvHelpS2P1: 'To find the resultant analytically, we resolve each force into two components (horizontal and vertical):',
    lvHelpS2M1: 'Horizontal components (X): ΣFₓ = F₁·cos(θ₁) + F₂·cos(θ₂)',
    lvHelpS2M2: 'Vertical components (Y): ΣFᵧ = F₁·sin(θ₁) + F₂·sin(θ₂)',
    lvHelpS2M3: 'Resultant magnitude (F_R): F_R = √(ΣFₓ² + ΣFᵧ²)',
    lvHelpS2M4: 'Resultant direction (φ): φ = tan⁻¹(ΣFᵧ / ΣFₓ)',
    lvHelpS2M5: 'Equilibrant angle: θ_E = φ + 180°',
    lvHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    lvHelpS3L1: 'Define two forces: Choose two force values (via known masses, where F = m·g) and two different angles (e.g., F₁ = 2 N at 0°, F₂ = 3 N at 120°).',
    lvHelpS3L2: 'Observe imbalance: The central ring moves away from center due to the resultant force.',
    lvHelpS3L3: 'Experimental balancing: Add masses (third force F_E) and gradually change its angle until the central ring returns to center, free and not touching the central axis.',
    lvHelpS3L4: 'Record results: Record the magnitude of the third force and the angle that achieved complete equilibrium.',
    lvHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis & Calculating the Unknown',
    lvHelpS4P1: 'In this experiment, we use the Vector Polygon / Parallelogram Method to verify the unknown:',
    lvHelpS4L1: 'Parallelogram method: Choose a suitable scale (e.g., 1 N = 2 cm). Draw vector F⃗₁ at its angle, and from the same origin draw F⃗₂ at its angle. Complete the parallelogram. The diagonal from the origin represents the resultant graphically (F⃗_R).',
    lvHelpS4L2: 'Calculating the unknown: Measure the diagonal length with a ruler and convert to Newtons, measure its angle with a protractor. Compare graphical and theoretical values with the equilibrant force (F_E) found experimentally to verify: F_E = F_R and θ_E = φ ± 180°',
    lvHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    lvHelpS5E1: 'Independent variables: Magnitudes and angles of the first and second forces (F₁, θ₁, F₂, θ₂)',
    lvHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variables: Equilibrant force and its angle (F_E, θ_E) needed to achieve equilibrium',
    lvHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Gravitational acceleration (g) and the central equilibrium point',
    lvHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    lvHelpS6L1: 'Applied understanding of vector addition geometrically and analytically rather than simple algebraic addition.',
    lvHelpS6L2: 'Understanding principles of statics and equilibrium, the fundamental principle in civil and architectural engineering for designing bridges and buildings to prevent collapse under forces.',
    // ── Mirror Help Modal ──
    miHelpTitle: '🪞 Spherical Mirrors Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    miHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    miHelpS1P1: 'Spherical mirrors are divided into two types based on the reflecting surface:',
    miHelpS1L1: 'Concave (Converging) Mirror: The reflecting surface is curved inward. It converges parallel rays to a point called the real focal point (F). Image characteristics change (real inverted, or virtual magnified) depending on object position relative to the focal point.',
    miHelpS1L2: 'Convex (Diverging) Mirror: The reflecting surface is curved outward. It diverges incident rays, forming a virtual focal point (F) behind the mirror. Image characteristics are always the same (virtual, upright, diminished) regardless of object position.',
    miHelpS1P2: 'The fundamental principle is based on the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applied to a curved surface, where object distance (u) and image distance (v) are related to the mirror focal length (f).',
    miHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    miHelpS2P1: 'Mirror Equation:',
    miHelpS2P2: '(where u is the object distance from the mirror pole, v is the image distance, and f is the focal length).',
    miHelpS2P3: 'Sign Convention:',
    miHelpS2L1: 'u is always positive for real objects.',
    miHelpS2L2: 'f is positive for concave mirrors, negative for convex mirrors.',
    miHelpS2L3: 'v is positive if the image is real (in front of mirror), negative if virtual (behind mirror).',
    miHelpS2P4: 'Magnification (M):',
    miHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    miHelpS3P1: 'We focus on the concave mirror because it allows obtaining real images that can be received on a screen:',
    miHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Place a light source (arrow-shaped object or candle) in front of a concave mirror with unknown focal length.',
    miHelpS3L2: 'Set object distance (u): Place the object at a known first distance (e.g., u = 30 cm) such that the distance is greater than the expected focal length.',
    miHelpS3L3: 'Determine image distance (v): Move the screen in front of the mirror back and forth until the sharpest inverted image forms on it, then measure the distance from mirror to screen accurately and record it as (v).',
    miHelpS3L4: 'Repeat: Change the object distance (u) to several different values (35 cm, 40 cm, 45 cm, 50 cm), and each time find the corresponding image distance (v) and record data in a table.',
    miHelpS3L5: 'Reciprocals: Calculate the reciprocal of object distance (1/u) and image distance (1/v) for each reading.',
    miHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    miHelpS4P1: 'The goal of the graphical analysis is to find the unknown focal length of the mirror (f).',
    miHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot reciprocal of image distance (1/v) on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of object distance (1/u) on the X-axis.',
    miHelpS4L2: 'Graph nature & slope: You get a straight line sloping downward (inverse relationship between reciprocals), with slope equal to −1: Slope = −1',
    miHelpS4L3: 'Calculating f: From the mirror equation: 1/v = −1/u + 1/f. The Y-intercept and X-intercept both represent 1/f. Read the Y-intercept (let its value be C). Calculate the unknown focal length: f = 1/C',
    miHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    miHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable: Object distance from mirror (u)',
    miHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable: Formed image distance (v)',
    miHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Mirror focal length (f), radius of curvature (R = 2f), and original object height (hₒ)',
    miHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    miHelpS6L1: 'Determining the focal length and radius of curvature of spherical mirrors practically.',
    miHelpS6L2: 'Understanding different image formation cases based on object position relative to center of curvature (C) and focal point (F).',
    miHelpS6L3: 'Practical applications include using concave mirrors in car headlights and telescopes to collect light, and using convex mirrors on car sides and road corners to provide a wide field of view.',
    // ── ThinLens Help Modal ──
    tlHelpTitle: '🔍 Thin Lens Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    tlHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    tlHelpS1P1: 'Thin lenses are classified based on their geometry and effect on rays into two types:',
    tlHelpS1L1: 'Convex (Converging) Lens: Thicker at the center and thinner at the edges. It converges parallel light rays to a point called the real focal point (F). Image characteristics change (real inverted, or virtual magnified) depending on object position.',
    tlHelpS1L2: 'Concave (Diverging) Lens: Thinner at the center and thicker at the edges. It diverges incident rays, and has a virtual focal point (F). Image characteristics are always the same (virtual, upright, diminished).',
    tlHelpS1P2: 'This behavior follows the general lens equation relating object distance (u), image distance (v), and lens focal length (f).',
    tlHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    tlHelpS2P1: 'Gaussian Lens Formula:',
    tlHelpS2P2: '(where u is the object distance from the optical center, v is the image distance, and f is the focal length).',
    tlHelpS2P3: 'Sign convention for lenses:',
    tlHelpS2L1: 'f is positive for convex (converging) lenses, negative for concave (diverging) lenses.',
    tlHelpS2L2: 'v is positive if the image is real (formed on the other side of the lens), negative if virtual (on the same side as the object).',
    tlHelpS2P4: 'Magnification (M):',
    tlHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    tlHelpS3P1: 'We apply the experiment on the convex lens because it allows forming real images that can be observed on a screen:',
    tlHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Place the light source (object), then the convex lens with unknown focal length, then the white screen on a straight line.',
    tlHelpS3L2: 'Set object distance (u): Place the object at a known distance from the lens (e.g., u = 20 cm).',
    tlHelpS3L3: 'Determine image distance (v): Move the screen behind the lens back and forth until the sharpest inverted image appears, then measure the distance from lens to screen and record it as (v).',
    tlHelpS3L4: 'Repeat: Change the object distance (u) to several different values (25 cm, 30 cm, 35 cm, 40 cm), and each time find the corresponding image distance (v).',
    tlHelpS3L5: 'Calculate reciprocals: Calculate the reciprocals of distances (1/u) and (1/v) for all trials.',
    tlHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    tlHelpS4P1: 'The goal is to determine the unknown focal length of the lens (f) graphically.',
    tlHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Plot reciprocal of image distance (1/v) on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of object distance (1/u) on the X-axis.',
    tlHelpS4L2: 'Graph nature & slope: Due to the inverse relationship between reciprocals, you get a straight line sloping downward with slope: Slope = −1',
    tlHelpS4L3: 'Calculating f: From the equation: 1/v = −1/u + 1/f. The Y-intercept or X-intercept represents 1/f. Identify the Y-intercept (let it be C). Calculate the lens focal length: f = 1/C',
    tlHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    tlHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable: Object distance from lens (u)',
    tlHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable: Formed image distance (v)',
    tlHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Lens focal length (f), and lens power (P = 1/f)',
    tlHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    tlHelpS6L1: 'Calculating the focal length and power of convex lenses practically.',
    tlHelpS6L2: 'Understanding how to control image characteristics (magnified, diminished, same size) by changing object position.',
    tlHelpS6L3: 'Enormous real-life applications in manufacturing eyeglasses (for treating near and farsightedness), cameras, microscopes, and telescopes.',
    // ── Prism Help Modal ──
    prHelpTitle: '🌈 Prism Dispersion Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    prHelpS1Title: '🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory',
    prHelpS1P1: 'This experiment relies on the phenomenon of Dispersion. When white light (like sunlight) passes from a medium with a small refractive index (air) to a medium with a larger refractive index (glass or acrylic prism), it undergoes Refraction.',
    prHelpS1P2: 'White light is not a single color, but a mixture of the seven visible spectrum colors. The fundamental physical principle here is that the refractive index of glass (n) depends on the wavelength (λ) of light passing through it, known as Cauchy\'s Equation:',
    prHelpS1P3: 'Since different colors have different wavelengths:',
    prHelpS1L1: 'Red light: Has the largest wavelength (λ), thus encounters the lowest refractive index, making it the least deviated color.',
    prHelpS1L2: 'Violet light: Has the shortest wavelength (λ), thus encounters the highest refractive index, making it the most deviated color.',
    prHelpS1P4: 'Due to this difference in refraction angles, white light exits the prism dispersed into the seven spectrum colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).',
    prHelpS2Title: '📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used',
    prHelpS2P1: 'Snell\'s Law:',
    prHelpS2P2: 'Angle of Deviation (δ): The angle between the incident ray extension and the emerging ray from the prism, calculated at minimum deviation position:',
    prHelpS2P3: '(where A is the prism apex angle, and δₘ is the minimum angle of deviation).',
    prHelpS3Title: '⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)',
    prHelpS3L1: 'Setup: Place the glass prism in the light path, and have the light source emit a narrow beam of white light.',
    prHelpS3L2: 'Observe dispersion: Adjust the incidence angle until the light beam exits the other end of the prism clearly dispersed into rainbow colors on the dark screen.',
    prHelpS3L3: 'Change light type (for calculations): For precise data, switch the light source to monochromatic light, starting with a specific color (e.g., red, where wavelength is precisely known λ ≈ 650 nm).',
    prHelpS3L4: 'Measure deviation angle: Gradually change the incidence angle until reaching the minimum possible deviation angle for the emerging ray, and record the minimum deviation angle (δₘ).',
    prHelpS3L5: 'Repeat for other colors: Repeat with different colors (yellow, green, blue, violet) and record δₘ for each, then use the prism equation to calculate the refractive index (n) for each color (wavelength).',
    prHelpS4Title: '📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    prHelpS4P1: 'The goal is to find the relationship between refractive index and wavelength to verify the prism material constants (Cauchy constants A and B).',
    prHelpS4L1: 'Axes: Calculate the reciprocal of squared wavelength (1/λ²) for each color. Plot refractive index (n) on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of squared wavelength (1/λ²) on the X-axis.',
    prHelpS4L2: 'Slope: You get a straight line rising upward, its slope represents constant B in Cauchy\'s equation: Slope = Δn / Δ(1/λ²) = B',
    prHelpS4L3: 'Calculating the unknown: Constant B = slope value directly. Constant A (refractive index at infinite wavelength) = Y-intercept',
    prHelpS5Title: '⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    prHelpS5E1: 'Independent variable: Wavelength of the used beam (λ)',
    prHelpS5E2: 'Dependent variable: Minimum deviation angle (δₘ) and thus refractive index (n)',
    prHelpS5E3: 'Constants: Prism apex angle (A), and glass material',
    prHelpS6Title: '🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    prHelpS6L1: 'Understanding the nature of white light and proving it consists of multiple spectral components.',
    prHelpS6L2: 'Calculating material refractive indices precisely based on colors.',
    prHelpS6L3: 'Practical applications include manufacturing spectrometers used for material analysis, and determining chemical composition of distant stars by analyzing their received light.',
    // ── Diffraction Help Modal ──
    dfHelpTitle: '🔮 Light Diffraction Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    dfHelpS1Title: '🔧 1. Detailed Apparatus Description',
    dfHelpS1L1: 'Optical Bench: A long graduated metal rail on which all components are mounted to ensure perfect alignment on a single optical axis and prevent any lateral ray deviation.',
    dfHelpS1L2: 'Monochromatic Laser Source: Preferably a red laser (known wavelength, e.g., λ = 632.8 nm) or green laser. Its advantage is producing a coherent beam with constant phase and wavelength, essential for clear diffraction patterns.',
    dfHelpS1L3: 'Diffraction Slit Disk/Plate: A glass or metal slide containing precise micrometer-sized openings. In this experiment we use a Single Slit with known width denoted (a) measured in micrometers (μm).',
    dfHelpS1L4: 'Observation Screen: A flat white screen placed at a relatively large distance from the slit, where diffraction fringes (bright and dark regions) appear clearly.',
    dfHelpS1L5: 'Digital Caliper / Micrometer: A very precise measuring tool used to measure distances between dark fringes on the screen with high accuracy in millimeters.',
    dfHelpS2Title: '🔬 2. Detailed Scientific Theory',
    dfHelpS2P1: 'According to traditional geometric optics, light travels in straight lines, so if it passes through a small slit it should appear on the screen as a bright rectangle with the same dimensions as the slit. But in reality, when the slit width (a) is very small and close to the light wavelength (λ), light bends and spreads at the slit edges in different directions; this phenomenon is called Diffraction.',
    dfHelpS2P2: 'The secondary waves resulting from light bending (based on Huygens\' principle) interfere to form a distinctive pattern on the screen called a Diffraction Pattern, consisting of:',
    dfHelpS2L1: 'Central Maximum: A very wide bright fringe at the exact center with the highest intensity.',
    dfHelpS2L2: 'Secondary dark and bright fringes: Distributed on both sides of the central maximum, with intensity and fringe width decreasing away from center.',
    dfHelpS2P3: 'The first dark fringe occurs at a vertical distance (y) from center when destructive interference condition is met, meaning path difference equals one full wavelength.',
    dfHelpS3Title: '📐 3. Mathematical Equations Used',
    dfHelpS3P1: 'Condition for dark fringes in diffraction:',
    dfHelpS3P2: '(where a is slit width, θ is diffraction angle, m is dark fringe order m = ±1, ±2, …, and λ is wavelength).',
    dfHelpS3P3: 'Small angle approximation:',
    dfHelpS3P4: 'Linear equation used in the experiment (for first order m=1):',
    dfHelpS4Title: '⚗️ 4. Detailed Laboratory Procedure',
    dfHelpS4L1: 'Setup and calibration: Mount the laser at the start of the optical bench, followed by the slit holder, then place the white screen at the end at a large known distance (measure distance D between slit and screen with a ruler and keep it constant, e.g., D = 1.5 meter).',
    dfHelpS4L2: 'System operation: Turn on the laser beam and aim it precisely through the first single slit with known width (start with the narrowest slit, e.g., a = 0.04 mm).',
    dfHelpS4L3: 'Observe and read pattern: You will notice a horizontal line of bright and dark fringes on the screen. Identify the center of the central bright maximum, then use the digital caliper to measure the distance from center to the first dark fringe (m=1) on the right side, and record this distance as (y). (For better precision, measure the distance between the first dark fringes on both sides and divide by 2).',
    dfHelpS4L4: 'Change slit width: Rotate the slit disk to switch to another single slit with a different larger width (0.08 mm, 0.12 mm, 0.16 mm), and each time measure the corresponding first dark fringe distance (y). You will notice experimentally that as the slit widens, the diffraction pattern narrows and fringes move closer to center.',
    dfHelpS4L5: 'Calculations: Arrange slit width values (a) in a table, then calculate the reciprocal of slit width (1/a) for all readings to prepare for linear plotting.',
    dfHelpS5Title: '📊 5. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    dfHelpS5P1: 'The goal of the graph is to verify the wave nature and extract the laser wavelength (λ) as an experimental unknown.',
    dfHelpS5L1: 'Axes: Plot first dark fringe distance (y) in millimeters on the Y-axis. Plot reciprocal of slit width (1/a) in inverse millimeters on the X-axis.',
    dfHelpS5L2: 'Slope: You get a straight line passing through the origin showing direct proportionality between y and (1/a), calculate its slope: Slope = Δy / Δ(1/a)',
    dfHelpS5L3: 'Calculating λ: By comparison with the theoretical equation (y = λD · 1/a), we find the slope equals: Slope = λ · D. Since the screen distance (D) is known and constant, extract the unknown wavelength: λ = Slope / D',
    dfHelpS6Title: '⚙️ 6. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    dfHelpS6E1: 'Independent variable: Single slit width (a) and thus its reciprocal (1/a)',
    dfHelpS6E2: 'Dependent variable: Position or distance of first dark fringe from center (y)',
    dfHelpS6E3: 'Constants: Distance between slit and screen (D), and laser wavelength (λ)',
    dfHelpS7Title: '🎯 7. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    dfHelpS7L1: 'Definitively proving the wave behavior of light and refuting the idea that light travels in absolutely straight lines at microscopic edges.',
    dfHelpS7L2: 'The ability to measure very small dimensions (such as light wavelengths or thin wire and hair diameters) with micrometer precision by observing their diffraction patterns.',
    dfHelpS7L3: 'Enormous technological applications; setting fundamental limits for microscope resolution, controlling electronic chip and processor design (Photolithography), and used in studying crystalline structure of materials via X-ray diffraction.',

    ifHelpS7L1: 'Definitively proving the wave behavior of light through interference, one of the strongest evidences for the wave nature of light.',

    // ── SpeedOfSound Help Modal ──
    ssHelpTitle: '🔊 Speed of Sound Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    ssHelpS1Title: '🔧 1. Detailed Apparatus Description',
    ssHelpS1L1: 'Resonance Tube: A long transparent tube graduated in centimeters and meters, placed vertically and partially filled with water. The lower end is connected to a flexible hose, while the upper end is completely open to air.',
    ssHelpS1L2: 'Water Reservoir: A container connected to the tube via a plastic hose, can be raised and lowered manually on a metal stand. Its function is to control the water level inside the tube precisely, thus controlling the air column length (L).',
    ssHelpS1L3: 'Tuning Forks Set: A set of metal tuning forks, each engraved with its specific constant frequency (e.g., 256 Hz, 320 Hz, 512 Hz). They generate pure sound waves of constant frequency.',
    ssHelpS1L4: 'Rubber Hammer/Striker: A small hammer with a soft rubber head, used to strike the tuning fork tines gently to generate vibration without damaging the fork or causing metallic noise.',
    ssHelpS1L5: 'Level Indicator: A small movable ring on the tube used to mark the exact water surface position when resonance is heard, to facilitate reading the length from the graduated scale.',
    ssHelpS2Title: '🔬 2. Comprehensive Scientific Theory',
    ssHelpS2P1: 'Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that travels through air as compressions and rarefactions. When the tuning fork vibrates at the open end of the tube, it sends sound waves that travel down the tube until they hit the closed surface (water) and reflect back upward.',
    ssHelpS2P2: 'The incident wave interferes with the reflected wave both constructively and destructively, leading to the formation of a Standing Wave within the air column.',
    ssHelpS2L1: 'Node: Always forms at the water surface (closed end) because air particles are constrained.',
    ssHelpS2L2: 'Antinode: Forms at the tube opening (open end) where air particles have maximum freedom to vibrate.',
    ssHelpS2P3: 'When the air column length (L) matches the conditions for standing wave formation, the phenomenon of Resonance occurs, which is the state of maximum sound energy flow, resulting in a clear and very loud amplified sound.',
    ssHelpS2P4: 'The first resonance occurs when the tube contains exactly one quarter of a full wavelength:',
    ssHelpS2P5: 'Since the actual antinode forms slightly outside the top edge of the tube, an end correction factor (e) is added:',
    ssHelpS3Title: '📐 3. Mathematical Equations Used',
    ssHelpS3P1: 'Fundamental wave relation:',
    ssHelpS3P2: 'First resonance linear equation:',
    ssHelpS3P3: 'By substituting the wavelength (λ) into the length equation (L), we get the direct equation for graphing:',
    ssHelpS3P4: '(where L is the air column length in meters, v is the speed of sound, f is the frequency, and e is the end correction factor).',
    ssHelpS4Title: '⚗️ 4. Detailed Laboratory Procedure',
    ssHelpS4L1: 'System preparation: Ensure the water reservoir is filled to about the middle of the tube, and check for any water leaks in the hose.',
    ssHelpS4L2: 'Select first tuning fork: Choose a tuning fork with known frequency (start with the lowest frequency, e.g., f = 256 Hz, as it gives a large wavelength that is easy to observe).',
    ssHelpS4L3: 'Excite the fork: Strike the tuning fork tines gently with the rubber hammer, then quickly hold it horizontally so the vibrating tines are directly above the tube opening without touching it.',
    ssHelpS4L4: 'Search for resonance: While the fork is vibrating, slowly lower the water reservoir to increase the air column length. Listen carefully until you notice a sudden, strong amplification of the tone.',
    ssHelpS4L5: 'Determine the length: At the point of loudest sound, secure the reservoir and place the level indicator at the water surface. Read the distance from the top edge of the tube to the indicator and record it as (L).',
    ssHelpS4L6: 'Change frequencies: Repeat the entire process using the remaining tuning forks (320 Hz, 384 Hz, 512 Hz), and each time record the corresponding length (L).',
    ssHelpS4L7: 'Calculations: Create a table with the frequencies (f), then calculate the reciprocal of each frequency (1/f) to prepare the data for graphing.',
    ssHelpS5Title: '📊 5. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    ssHelpS5P1: 'The primary goal is to extract the speed of sound (v) under current laboratory conditions.',
    ssHelpS5L1: 'Axes: Plot the air column length (L) on the Y-axis. Plot the reciprocal of frequency (1/f) on the X-axis.',
    ssHelpS5L2: 'Slope: You will notice the points form a straight line rising upward that does not pass through the origin (it intersects the Y-axis on the negative side). Calculate the slope: Slope = ΔL / Δ(1/f)',
    ssHelpS5L3: 'Calculating v: By comparison with the equation L = (v/4)·(1/f) − e, we find: Slope = v / 4. Therefore, the unknown speed of sound is calculated by multiplying the slope by 4: v = 4 × Slope',
    ssHelpS5L4: 'Note: The Y-intercept on the negative side represents the end correction factor (e).',
    ssHelpS6Title: '⚙️ 6. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    ssHelpS6E1: 'Independent variable: Frequency of the tuning fork used (f) and thus its reciprocal (1/f)',
    ssHelpS6E2: 'Dependent variable: Air column length (L) resulting from water level change',
    ssHelpS6E3: 'Constants: Air temperature in the laboratory (since the speed of sound changes with temperature)',
    ssHelpS7Title: '🎯 7. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    ssHelpS7L1: 'Calculating the actual and practical value of the speed of sound in air in your environment and comparing it with the standard theoretical value (≈ 343 m/s at 20°C).',
    ssHelpS7L2: 'Understanding the principle of "standing waves" and resonance, which is the operational and physical principle behind all wind musical instruments (such as flutes, clarinets, and organ pipes).',
    // ── Polarization Help Modal ──
    poHelpTitle: '�️ Light Polarization Experiment Guide — Complete Guide',
    poHelpS1Title: '🔧 1. Detailed Apparatus Description',
    poHelpS1L1: 'Optical Bench: A long heavy metal ruler mounted on the table, with sliding tracks for mounting optical components. Its function is to maintain a straight and uniform optical axis for all instruments to prevent ray scattering.',
    poHelpS1L2: 'Light Source: A halogen lamp or laser emitting an intense light beam. This light is unpolarized, meaning its electric fields vibrate in all possible directions perpendicular to the beam propagation line.',
    poHelpS1L3: 'Polarizer: An optical filter made of polymer material containing microscopic longitudinal molecules aligned in one direction called the Transmission Axis. It only allows light waves vibrating parallel to this axis to pass through, producing linearly polarized light.',
    poHelpS1L4: 'Analyzer: A second polarizing filter identical to the first, mounted in a circular disc graduated from 0° to 360° allowing manual rotation with precision. Its function is to control the amount of transmitted light and test the polarization angle.',
    poHelpS1L5: 'Light Intensity Sensor: A digital photodetector placed at the end of the optical bench, receiving the transmitted light and converting its optical energy into an accurate digital reading of light intensity.',
    poHelpS2Title: '🔬 2. Detailed Scientific Theory',
    poHelpS2P1: 'Light consists of perpendicular electric and magnetic fields oscillating in space. When unpolarized light passes through the first polarizer, its intensity halves and it gains a single fixed vibration angle, called Linearly Polarized Light with initial intensity denoted I₀.',
    poHelpS2P2: 'When this polarized light strikes the second polarizer (Analyzer), its transmission depends entirely on the angle (θ) between the transmission axes of the polarizer and analyzer:',
    poHelpS2L1: 'θ = 0° (axes parallel): All light passes through and intensity is at its maximum.',
    poHelpS2L2: 'θ = 90° (axes perpendicular): The analyzer absorbs all polarized light and intensity is completely zero (total blackout).',
    poHelpS2P3: 'This relationship is governed by Malus\'s Law, which states that the transmitted light intensity is directly proportional to the square of the cosine of the rotation angle between the two axes.',
    poHelpS3Title: '📐 3. Mathematical Equations Used',
    poHelpS3P1: 'Malus\'s Law (fundamental):',
    poHelpS3P2: '(where I is the transmitted light intensity measured by the sensor, I₀ is the maximum intensity at parallel alignment, and θ is the analyzer rotation angle).',
    poHelpS4Title: '⚗️ 4. Detailed Laboratory Procedure',
    poHelpS4L1: 'Setup: Arrange the apparatus on the optical bench in the following order: Light Source ← Fixed Polarizer ← Rotatable Analyzer ← Light Intensity Sensor. Ensure the rays pass exactly through the centers of the components.',
    poHelpS4L2: 'Zero calibration (I₀): Turn on the light source, and rotate the analyzer until you find the highest intensity reading. Fix the analyzer at this position and set the circular disc to angle θ = 0°. Record this maximum intensity as (I₀).',
    poHelpS4L3: 'Data collection: Rotate the analyzer by 10° and record the new light intensity value (I).',
    poHelpS4L4: 'Extended observation: Continue rotating the analyzer in fixed steps (20°, 30°, 40°...) and you will notice the intensity decreasing until reaching 90° where the reading is zero (blackout). Continue to 180° to witness the intensity return to maximum.',
    poHelpS4L5: 'Calculations: Create a table containing the angles (θ) and corresponding intensity (I). Calculate the cosine of each angle cos(θ) then square it to obtain cos²(θ) values.',
    poHelpS5Title: '📊 5. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown',
    poHelpS5L1: 'Axes: Plot the measured light intensity (I) on the Y-axis. Plot the squared cosine value (cos²θ) on the X-axis.',
    poHelpS5L2: 'Slope: Due to the linear direct proportionality between I and cos²θ, the points form a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope is calculated by: Slope = ΔI / Δcos²θ',
    poHelpS5L3: 'Calculating the unknown: By comparison with Malus\'s Law (I = I₀ cos²θ), we find that the graphically obtained slope directly represents the unknown maximum initial intensity: Slope = I₀',
    poHelpS6Title: '⚙️ 6. Constants & Variables in the Experiment',
    poHelpS6E1: 'Independent variable: Graduated analyzer angle (θ)',
    poHelpS6E2: 'Dependent variable: Transmitted light intensity (I)',
    poHelpS6E3: 'Constants: Original lamp intensity (I₀), distance between instruments, type of polarization filters',
    poHelpS7Title: '🎯 7. Scientific Importance & Benefits',
    poHelpS7L1: 'Proving that light is a transverse wave (since longitudinal waves like sound cannot be polarized at all).',
    poHelpS7L2: 'Enormous everyday applications: manufacturing LCD screens (relying on changing liquid crystal polarization with electric voltage), and polarized sunglasses to block glare reflected from water and road surfaces.',

  // ── FreeFall Help Modal ──
  ffHelpTitle: "📖 Free Fall Experiment Guide — Complete Guide",
  ffHelpS1Title: "🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory",
  ffHelpS1P1: "Free fall is the motion of a body under the influence of Earth's gravity alone, neglecting air resistance. In this case, all bodies (regardless of mass) acquire the same constant acceleration, called gravitational acceleration, denoted by g.",
  ffHelpS1P2: "This motion follows the equations of linear motion with constant acceleration. If the body starts from rest (initial velocity v₀ = 0) and falls a vertical distance y in time t, the equation relating distance to time is:",
  ffHelpS2Title: "📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used",
  ffHelpS2M1: "Distance-time equation: y = ½ · g · t²",
  ffHelpS2M2: "Final velocity-time equation: v = g · t",
  ffHelpS2M3: "Velocity-distance equation: v² = 2 · g · y",
  ffHelpS2M4: "Extracting g from one measurement: g = 2y / t²",
  ffHelpS3Title: "⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual or Real)",
  ffHelpS3L1: "Equipment setup: Mount the graduated ruler vertically, place the ball (or falling object) at the starting point (zero height), and prepare the electronic timer (or photogates for precise time measurement).",
  ffHelpS3L2: "Set the height (y): Choose a specific height (e.g., 0.2 m, 0.4 m, 0.6 m, etc.).",
  ffHelpS3L3: "Release & measure: Let the object fall freely (from rest), and record the time (t) taken to reach the ground or photogate.",
  ffHelpS3L4: "Repetition: Repeat the step for each height 3 times and calculate the average time to reduce experimental error.",
  ffHelpS3L5: "Square the time: Calculate the square of the average time (t²) for each height.",
  ffHelpS4Title: "📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown",
  ffHelpS4P1: "To find the value of gravitational acceleration (g) scientifically from the graph:",
  ffHelpS4L1: "Axes: Plot distance (y) on the Y-axis. Plot time squared (t²) on the X-axis.",
  ffHelpS4L2: "Slope: When plotting the relationship, you get a straight line through the origin. Calculate its slope: Slope = Δy / Δt²",
  ffHelpS4L3: "Calculating g: Comparing with the theoretical equation (y = ½gt²), the slope equals half the gravitational acceleration: Slope = ½ · g → g = 2 × Slope",
  ffHelpS5Title: "⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment",
  ffHelpS5E1: "Independent variable (controlled): Height (y)",
  ffHelpS5E2: "Dependent variable (changes with height): Time (t) and thus (t²)",
  ffHelpS5E3: "Constant to calculate and verify: Gravitational acceleration (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²)",
  ffHelpS6Title: "🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits",
  ffHelpS6L1: "Proving that free fall acceleration is constant for all bodies and independent of mass (neglecting air).",
  ffHelpS6L2: "Calculating the practical value of gravitational acceleration (g) at the experiment location and comparing it with the standard value.",

  // ── Spring Help Modal ──
  spHelpTitle: "🌀 Spring Oscillation Experiment Guide — Complete Guide",
  spHelpS1Title: "🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory",
  spHelpS1P1: "When a mass (m) is hung on a vertically suspended spring, the mass pulls the spring downward with its weight, while an opposing elastic force is generated in the spring trying to restore it to its original position, called the Restoring Force.",
  spHelpS1P2: "This force follows Hooke's Law, which states that the restoring force is directly proportional to the extension (x) in the spring:",
  spHelpS1P3: "Where (k) is the Spring Constant measured in (N/m). When the mass is displaced from its equilibrium and released, it moves in simple harmonic motion (SHM) up and down with a constant period that depends on the mass and spring stiffness.",
  spHelpS2Title: "📐 2. Mathematical Equations Used",
  spHelpS2M1: "Hooke's Law (static case): m · g = k · x",
  spHelpS2M2: "Period of spring oscillation (T): T = 2π √(m / k)",
  spHelpS2M3: "Squaring both sides for a linear relation: T² = (4π² / k) · m",
  spHelpS2M4: "Angular frequency (ω₀): ω₀ = √(k / m)",
  spHelpS2M5: "Total energy of the system: E = ½ · k · A²",
  spHelpS3Title: "⚗️ 3. Laboratory Procedure (Virtual)",
  spHelpS3L1: "Fix the spring: Choose a spring with a specified stiffness constant (k) in the system.",
  spHelpS3L2: "Change the mass (m): Hang a known mass (e.g., 0.1 kg) on the spring.",
  spHelpS3L3: "Start oscillation & measure: Pull the mass down slightly and release. Measure the time of 10 complete oscillations with the digital timer, then divide by 10 to get the period (T) for one mass.",
  spHelpS3L4: "Repetition: Repeat the steps using different increasing masses (0.2 kg, 0.3 kg, 0.4 kg, 0.5 kg).",
  spHelpS3L5: "Square the results: Square the calculated period values to get (T²).",
  spHelpS4Title: "📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown",
  spHelpS4P1: "The goal of this section is to calculate the unknown spring constant (k) graphically.",
  spHelpS4L1: "Axes: Plot period squared (T²) on the Y-axis. Plot mass (m) on the X-axis.",
  spHelpS4L2: "Slope: You get a straight line through the origin, its slope is: Slope = ΔT² / Δm",
  spHelpS4L3: "Calculating k: Comparing with the theoretical equation (T² = 4π²/k · m), we find: Slope = 4π² / k, therefore: k = 4π² / Slope",
  spHelpS5Title: "⚙️ 5. Constants & Variables in the Experiment",
  spHelpS5E1: "Independent variable (controlled): Suspended mass (m)",
  spHelpS5E2: "Dependent variable (changes with mass): Oscillation period (T) and thus (T²)",
  spHelpS5E3: "Constants: Spring stiffness constant (k), and initial oscillation amplitude (displacement)",
  spHelpS6Title: "🎯 6. Scientific Importance & Benefits",
  spHelpS6L1: "Determining material elasticity (spring constant) and applying Hooke's Law practically.",

  spHelpS6L3: "Understanding mechanical systems based on springs widely used in engineering and automotive industry (suspensions).",

  pdHelpS1Title: "🔬 1. Introduction & Scientific Theory",
  pdHelpS1P1: "A simple pendulum consists of a point mass (m) suspended from a light, inextensible string of length (L). When displaced by a very small angle (θ < 10°) and released, it oscillates back and forth about its equilibrium in periodic motion known as Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).",

  pdHelpS2P3: "Frequency of the pendulum (f — Frequency):",

  pdHelpS4P1: "The main goal of this experiment is to calculate gravitational acceleration (g) practically.",

  // ── Projectile Help Modal ──

  pjHelpS1P1: "Projectile motion is the motion of a body launched into the air at an angle under the influence of gravity alone (neglecting air resistance). The fundamental principle here is motion independence, where projectile motion is split into two dimensions (2D):",

  pjHelpS1L2: "Vertical motion (Y-axis): with constant acceleration due to gravity (aᵧ = -g), where velocity decreases during ascent and increases during descent.",
  pjHelpS1P2: "If the projectile is launched with initial velocity v₀ at angle θ to the horizontal, the velocity components are:",

  pjHelpS3L3: "Launch & observe range: Each time, launch the projectile and measure the horizontal range (R) using the lab measurement tool.",

  pjHelpS4Title: "📊 4. Graphical Analysis, Slope & Calculating the Unknown",
  pjHelpS4P1: "To find the initial velocity (v₀) or verify gravitational acceleration (g) graphically:",
  pjHelpS4L1: "Axes: Plot horizontal range (R) on the Y-axis. Plot sin(2θ) on the X-axis.",

  pjHelpS4L3: "Calculating the unknown: Comparing with the equation (R = v₀²/g · sin(2θ)), we find: Slope = v₀² / g. If g is known (9.8 m/s²), you can calculate the unknown initial velocity: v₀ = √(Slope × g)",
